About: a resolved source keeps its surface brightness at every distance, and only absorption along the way dims it

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the observer's sky, a dark field 3° across with the Sun's disc at its centre at its true angular size, filled with the colour of a 5772 K blackbody. The dashed circle is the size of the Sun's disc seen from the Earth, 0.533°. With the screen on the field is seen through a faint grey tint. Right: the flux F, the solid angle Ω of the disc and their ratio F/Ω, each divided by its value at 1 AU with the screen off, on logarithmic axes against the distance d; the curves fill in wherever the observer has been, and the planets' initials mark their distances.
Controls
The distance slider moves the observer from 0.35 to 32 AU on a logarithmic scale. Each planet button carries the observer to that planet's mean distance (semi-major axis) in about 2 s. The screen toggle puts an absorbing screen of optical depth τ = 1 in front of the observer; it travels with the observer.
Measured
F, the angular diameter, Ω and F/Ω for a uniformly bright Sun of L = 3.828×1026 W and R = 6.957×108 m with no limb darkening; the screen absorbs every frequency equally and emits nothing. The readouts also give F, Ω and F/Ω as fractions of their values at 1 AU with the screen off.
When it holds
The surface brightness F/Ω is the same at every distance only if nothing along the way absorbs or emits, and in ordinary, static space. Over cosmological distances the expansion of the universe dims it as (1 + z)4. Strictly, F/Ω equals the surface intensity times (1 + cos α)/2, which differs from it by less than one part in 104 (under 0.005 %) anywhere on the slider.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Flux at Jupiter

Set the observer at the Earth, 1.00 AU, with the screen off, and note the flux. Before pressing the button for Jupiter, at 5.20 AU, predict by what factor the flux will fall.

2 · Solid angle at Jupiter

Go back to the Earth with the screen off and note the angular diameter and the solid angle of the disc. Before pressing the button for Jupiter again, predict what happens to the solid angle of the disc.

3 · Brightness per patch at Neptune

Keep the screen off and start again at the Earth, noting the ratio of flux to solid angle. Before pressing the button for Neptune, at 30.07 AU, where the flux is about 1/900 of its value at the Earth, predict how bright each patch of the disc will look.

4 · Switching the screen on

Go back to the Earth. Before switching the screen on, predict what the observer sees.

5 · The screen on the way to Neptune

Keep the screen on, which travels with the observer, and start at the Earth. Before pressing the button for Neptune, predict the ratio of flux to solid angle at Neptune.

6 · What stays the same

Flux falls as 1/d2, and so does the solid angle of the disc, so their ratio, the surface brightness F/Ω, is the same from Mercury to Neptune. Distance makes the Sun smaller, not dimmer per patch.

Only something along the way, an absorber like the screen, changes the surface brightness. That is why a surface brightness measures the source itself, and why it can be compared at any distance.

This holds in ordinary, static space. Across cosmological distances the expansion of the universe does dim surface brightness, as (1 + z)4.

The Sun Seen from Every Planet

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Stand at any planet and look at the Sun. This sim paints the Sun's disc as that observer sees it, at its true angular size, and reads out the flux F, the solid angle Ω of the disc and their ratio F/Ω. An optional absorbing screen can be put in front of the observer.

What you'll learn

  • What F, Ω and F/Ω each measure.
  • What happens to them as the observer moves from Mercury to Neptune.
  • What the absorbing screen does.
  • Why the same reasoning applies to a galaxy.
The sim shows the Sun as one observer sees it, and reads out F, Ω and F/Ω for that view.

What's on screen

  • Observer's sky (left): a dark field 3° across with the Sun's disc at its true angular size, in the colour of a 5772 K blackbody. A dashed circle marks the size seen from the Earth, 0.533°. A grey tint appears when the screen is on.
  • Flux F (right): on log axes against d, divided by its value at 1 AU with the screen off. The curve fills in wherever the observer has been, and planet initials mark their distances.
  • Solid angle Ω (right): the same plot, drawn as a thick pale line.
  • F/Ω (right): the ratio, divided by its 1 AU value.
  • Readouts: d, the angular diameter 2α, F, Ω and F/Ω, then each of F, Ω and F/Ω as a fraction of its 1 AU value.

03

The disc and its three numbers

An observer at distance d from the centre of the Sun sees a disc of angular radius α, where sin α = R/d and R is the Sun's radius. The sim reads out the angular diameter 2α. The solid angle Ω of the disc is the area it covers on a unit sphere, Ω = 2π(1 − cos α).

The geometry of the disc. The observer's line of sight to each edge just grazes the Sun.

The flux F is the energy per second crossing unit area at the observer, in W m−2. The ratio F/Ω, the flux per unit solid angle, is the sim's measure of how bright a patch of the disc is. It is the frequency-integrated form of the quantity that the notes call the specific intensity (eq. 3.14), I = ∫Iν dν, averaged over the disc: the energy per unit area, time and solid angle.

At the opening distance, 1 AU, with the screen off, the sim gives 2α = 0.533°, F = 1361 W m−2, Ω = 6.79 × 10−5 sr and F/Ω = 2.00 × 107 W m−2 sr−1.

Key idea. F/Ω is the flux per unit solid angle, the brightness of a patch of the disc.
See itLook at the Sun from the Earth with the screen off. Watch for: the disc filling the dashed circle, with 2α = 0.533°, F = 1361 W m−2 and F/Ω = 2.00 × 107 W m−2 sr−1 in the Readouts.
04

Flux and solid angle both fall as 1/d²

A star that radiates equally in all directions spreads its energy over a sphere of area 4πd², so the flux is (notes, eq. 1.2 and Section 1.3):

The inverse-square law. For the Sun, with L = 4πR²σSBT⁴, the second form follows.

The solid angle falls in the same way. For a small angle, α ≈ R/d and Ω = 2π(1 − cos α) ≈ πα²:

The angular radius falls as 1/d, and the solid angle, which goes as α², as 1/d².
Twice the distance halves the width of the disc and quarters its solid angle.

At Jupiter (5.203 AU, shown as 5.20) the angular diameter falls from 0.533° to 0.102°, a factor 5.20. The flux falls from 1361 to 50.3 W m−2 and Ω from 6.79 × 10−5 to 2.51 × 10−6 sr, each by a factor 27.07 = 5.203². At Neptune the factor is 904.2, so F = 1.51 W m−2.

Key idea. F and Ω both fall as 1/d², while the angular diameter falls as 1/d.
See itCarry the observer from the Earth to Jupiter, with the screen off. Watch for: F and Ω both falling to 0.037 of their values at 1 AU, while 2α falls to 0.102°.
05

F/Ω is the same at every distance

Divide one result by the other and d cancels, which leaves only properties of the Sun's surface (notes, eq. 1.2, Section 3.3):

For T = 5772 K, σSBT⁴/π = 2.00 × 107 W m−2 sr−1, the readout at every distance.

Behind this is the constancy of the specific intensity along a ray (notes, eq. 3.15, Figure 30). Two small patches of areas dA1 and dA2 a distance d12 apart exchange the energy I1 dA1 (dA2/d12²) dt dν, counted as it leaves the first, and I2 dA2 (dA1/d12²) dt dν, counted as it arrives. In empty space the two are equal, so I1 = I2. The surface of a blackbody has F = πI (eq. 3.17), so I = σSBT⁴/π.

F and Ω fall together, so F/Ω stays level, from 0.35 to 32 AU.

At Neptune the flux is 1/904 of its value at 1 AU, and so is Ω, but F/Ω is still 2.00 × 107. The sim uses the exact finite disc, for which F/Ω = I(1 + cos α)/2. This is within 0.005 percent of I everywhere on the slider.

Key idea. In empty space F/Ω does not depend on d: distance shrinks the disc and does not dim a patch of it.
See itCarry the observer from the Earth to Neptune, with the screen off. Watch for: F and Ω both falling to about 0.0011 of their values at 1 AU, while F/Ω stays at 2.00 × 107 W m−2 sr−1 and its fraction of the 1 AU value stays 1.00.
06

Only absorption changes F/Ω

A beam that crosses an optical depth τ is weakened by the factor e−τ (notes, Section 3.3, eq. 3.23):

The sim's screen has τ = 1 at every frequency, so the factor is e−1 = 0.368. It emits nothing.

At 1 AU with the screen on, the disc keeps its size, 2α = 0.533°, and so Ω is unchanged. F falls from 1361 to 501 W m−2 and F/Ω from 2.00 × 107 to 7.37 × 106, both by the factor 0.368.

The screen is in front of the observer, so it travels along. At Neptune the flux is again 1/904 of its value at 1 AU, 0.554 W m−2, but F/Ω is still 7.37 × 106, the same as at the Earth with the screen on. Flying away does not add a second absorption. The screen sets the brightness of a patch, and the distance sets its size.

Key idea. An absorber multiplies F/Ω by e−τ and leaves the size of the disc alone.
See itSwitch the screen on at the Earth. Watch for: the disc keeping its size, while F falls to 501 W m−2 and F/Ω to 7.37 × 106 W m−2 sr−1, both 0.368 of their values with the screen off.
See itWith the screen on, carry the observer from the Earth to Neptune. Watch for: F falling to 0.554 W m−2 while F/Ω stays at 7.37 × 106 W m−2 sr−1.
07

The same cancellation gives the surface brightness of a galaxy

A galaxy is described by its surface brightness ℐ, the luminosity emitted per unit projected area (notes, Section 8.1). A small patch of area dS at distance d emits the luminosity ℐ dS, so the flux from it is ℐ dS/4πd², and it subtends the solid angle dΩ = dS/d². Their ratio is:

Equation (8.1). The distance d has cancelled.

The flux falls as 1/d² and so does the solid angle over which it is spread, as for the Sun's disc. This is why the surface brightness of two galaxies can be compared without knowing their distances. It holds for galaxies near enough that the redshift of their light can be neglected.

Surface brightness is usually given in magnitudes per square arcsecond, msb = −2.5 log10 ℐ + constant, where a larger msb is a fainter surface. The faint outer parts of galaxies are measured against the night sky, about 22 mag arcsec−2 in the V band at a dark site. The sim does not show a galaxy, so this section has no See-it.

08

Summary

In one line. The flux per unit solid angle F/Ω is the brightness of a patch of the Sun's disc, and the sim shows how it responds to the observer's distance and to an absorbing screen.
  • F falls as 1/d² (eq. 1.2), and so does the solid angle Ω of the disc. The angular diameter falls as 1/d.
  • F/Ω = σSBT⁴/π = 2.00 × 107 W m−2 sr−1 from Mercury to Neptune: the specific intensity is constant along a ray in empty space.
  • An absorber of optical depth τ multiplies F/Ω by e−τ.
  • The same cancellation gives dF/dΩ = ℐ/4π for a galaxy (eq. 8.1).

Common mix-ups

  • "From Neptune the Sun is 900 times dimmer, so every patch is 900 times fainter." The flux is 1/904, but F/Ω is the same. The disc has become smaller.
  • "The solid angle falls like the angular diameter." It falls as 1/d², like the flux: 27.07 against 5.20 at Jupiter.
  • "Empty space dims the surface a little more at each planet." Only an absorber does.
  • "The screen shrinks the disc." It multiplies F and F/Ω by e−1 and leaves the angular size unchanged.

Things to try on your own

  • Fly from Mercury to Neptune with the screen on and watch F/Ω as a fraction of its 1 AU value with the screen off.
